one_line_input: Quiet Desk is a subscription service that ships a fresh mechanical keyboard switch set and a pre-cut desk mat combo every quarter, sized and dampened for people who work in shared apartments or thin-walled offices and don't want to bother roommates or coworkers with loud typing. Every switch set is chosen and lubed for low acoustic output at full typing speed, not just 'quiet marketing claims' - we publish actual decibel measurements for every switch we ship. Different from generic keyboard switch shops because we don't sell for feel or price first, we sell for measured sound output first, and everything is pre-lubed so there is no DIY lubing step. We refuse to look like a gamer-RGB aesthetic brand and refuse to look like a minimalist desk-setup Instagram aesthetic brand - this should feel like acoustic test equipment, not a lifestyle product.
positioning: Quiet Desk ships a quarterly, pre-lubed switch set and matched desk mat selected and tuned for measured sound output first, with a published decibel number for every switch — not feel, price, or an unverified 'quiet' marketing claim. Every researched general keyboard-parts shop (NovelKeys, Divinikey, KBDfans) organizes its catalog around feel, price, and build compatibility and treats 'quiet' as a tag, and the category's own most-used sound-comparison resource (Click and Thock) stops at subjective audio clips with zero decibel data; Quiet Desk is the one selling the number itself, on a recurring cadence, as the product.
audience: Someone who types for a living in a space they don't fully control the acoustics of — a shared apartment with a roommate, or a shared/thin-walled office — who has either already been told their typing is loud, or lost the private space that used to make it a non-issue, and switched to quieter gear reactively rather than by informed choice. They want to keep typing at full, normal speed; they don't want to become a keyboard hobbyist who learns to lube switches to get there.
tone: Reads like a lab report or a piece of test equipment's spec sheet — precise, plain, numeric, stating the measurement instead of an adjective. Confident without being sales-y: it doesn't need to hype 'whisper quiet,' it states the dB figure and lets that be the argument. Never sounds like: gamer hype copy ('unleash your setup', RGB energy), minimalist desk-aesthetic Instagram voice (soft, aspirational, lifestyle-first), or apologetic/precious language about being 'just' a subscription.
visual_pillars: Every asset that claims quiet shows the actual decibel figure in typographic focus (e.g. '38 dB @ 60 WPM'), never an unquantified adjective like 'whisper quiet' standing alone

Palette restricted to instrument/lab tones — matte black, neutral greys, one calibration accent (safety yellow or orange, like test equipment markings) — no RGB gradients and no soft pastel or beige lifestyle tones
Typography is monospace or a technical grotesk with spec-sheet numerals throughout — no display, script, or hand-lettered faces anywhere

Product photography treats switches and mats as measurement subjects — shot on a rig or plain surface with a scale/ruler reference, top-down or instrument-angle lighting — never a staged desk flat-lay with plants, coffee, or warm ambient light
Layouts read like dashboards or data sheets — tick marks, axis labels, waveform or dB-meter motifs — never soft rounded cards, Instagram-square crops, or mood-board collage layouts
Copy paired with any sound claim states the test condition (switch name, WPM, distance from mic) the way a spec sheet cites test conditions, not just the number alone
avoid: Gamer-RGB aesthetic — glossy renders, rainbow lighting, 'unleash'/'dominate' hype copy, esports visual language
Minimalist desk-setup Instagram aesthetic — soft flat-lays, plants, coffee cups, warm window light, aspirational lifestyle staging
Any 'quiet' or 'silent' claim stated as an adjective with no decibel figure attached — the category's own trusted comparison tool (Click and Thock) already stops there; Quiet Desk does not
Hobbyist/enthusiast catalog framing (feel-first language like 'buttery', 'thocky', endless variant browsing) that positions this as a build-your-own parts shop rather than a measured, curated product
Presenting the DIY-lubing step as something the customer is capable of or should consider — the entire value is that it's already done
Unsourced or single-source decibel benchmarks borrowed from third parties (e.g. citing another product's uncredited dB figure) — every number Quiet Desk publishes must be its own measurement
